source.title: Data-Induced Interactions of Sparse Sensors
source.authors: A. Klishin; J. Kutz; Krithika Manohar

record.tranche_reason: The study tests double-descent-shaped reconstruction-risk curves in sparse sensing, a different setting and measure from deep-network generalization.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own reconstruction-risk curves while varying sensor count. It also discusses double descent in deep learning, but cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows. Comparisons of sensor-placement energy alone are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own reconstruction-risk curves for linear sparse sensing as sensor count p varies. It finds a peak at p≈r for least-squares and unregularized QR reconstruction, and finds that prior regularization removes or suppresses it. This is a new setting, a linear inverse problem with fixed model rank r. Adding sensors (observations) near p=r raises error, which is the analogue of sample-wise 'more data hurts' (V3) and of regularization removing the peak (V6). Model capacity is not varied, so V4 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors report that unregularized (least squares, QR PS) reconstruction shows a double-descent peak when sensor count p matches mode count r. They conclude that their prior-regularized reconstruction suppresses it in the sensor-placement context, but does not fully explain the risk-curve shape. They leave optimal regularization design open.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates linear state reconstruction from sparse sensor measurements as sensor count varies, not deep-network test error as model size, training time, or sample size varies.
record.method_sensitivity: The risk-curve behavior changes with the sensor-placement prior and reconstruction prior; isotropic priors for both only partly suppress the peak, while the other three tested combinations remove it. The study also reports regularized versus unregularized reconstruction differences.
record.problems: The SST Fig. 3 prose and caption conflict about whether its risk curve has a peak. Much of the curve evidence is graphical rather than tabulated, and the paper does not establish that the regularization choices are optimal or explain the peak mechanism.
record.rows_left_out: No additional risk-curve results were left out.

untested.parts: Deep networks and model size: not studied.
Training-sample count for a learned model: the analogue here is the count of measurement sensors, with the training snapshot count fixed.
Varying capacity past the interpolation point: rank r is fixed throughout.
Effective-complexity measure predicting the peak location: not studied.
Whether label noise or variance drives the peak (noise level is not swept in the risk curves), multiple peaks, and whether the regularization is optimally tuned.
Recounting complexity by effective parameters: not studied.

missing.what: Per-dataset peak in the unregularized QR PS curves. The authors cite Olivetti in Fig. 4c as showing RMSE worsening at p≈r; no row isolates the dataset.
missing.locator: Section IV.D and Section V, Fig. 4c

record.verdict_notes: This is a linear inverse problem with fixed rank r; the axis varied is the number of measurements, not model capacity. Hence V4 links are removed and rows are relinked to V3, the sample-wise analogue, and to V6. The double-descent material is secondary to the paper's sensor-placement Ising-model contribution. The Fig. 3 prose and caption conflict, and all curve evidence is graphical. Noise level is fixed within each risk curve, so the role of noise in the peak is untested.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network test error across model sizes and the interpolation threshold.
Test error as training-sample count increases near interpolation.
The paper varies sensor count in sparse-sensing reconstruction; it does not test the generality of the curve across other model classes or establish a general classical U-shaped curve.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.

Whether noise or variance causes the peak, whether multiple peaks arise, and whether regularization is optimally tuned. The paper compares specified prior choices and reports their effects on the risk curve.
Recounting complexity by an effective number of parameters to determine whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

relationships.condition: Bayesian prior regularization in sparse sensing
relationships.reason: The POD-prior and POD-sensor combinations remove the peak (r3, r4, r5); regularized curves on other datasets lack it (r7, r8). A near-flat isotropic prior (σ=10^3) only slightly suppresses it (r2). Unregularized baselines show the peak (r1, r9).
relationships.display_finding: POD priors and sensors removed peaks, other regularized datasets also lacked peaks, and unregularized baselines retained them; an isotropic prior with σ=10³ provided only slight suppression.

tranche.reason: The study reports its own double-descent and regularization results in a new setting, linear reconstruction from sparse sensors, bearing on V6.

statements.correction: Axis: sensor count p; training snapshots: fixed within each sweep; three SST prior combinations: monotonic without a peak; regularized Olivetti: nearly monotonic; regularized cylinder: monotonic; V3: untested.
statements.problem: The monotonic or nearly monotonic reconstruction description is supported, but this study cannot supply a limits_scope verdict for V3 because it varies sensor count rather than training-set size.

statements.correction: Isotropic placement plus isotropic reconstruction: peak slightly suppressed, not removed; other three prior combinations: monotonic without a peak; regularized random, 2-point and QR methods: nearly equivalent RMSE curves in Section IV.D; early random-placement instability: not stated.
statements.problem: The prior-dependent SST findings are supported. An additional early instability caused by random placement is not established by the supplied text.
